newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ retail coffee prices seen up to 50 pct higher.
newsitem.headline: NZ retail coffee prices seen up to 50 pct higher.

text.p: A dramatic rise in world wholesale coffee prices has already started to affect consumers in New Zealand, and retail prices are expected to rise by as much as 50 percent, industry participants said on Friday.

"All the wholesalers have put up prices 15 to 20 percent, cafes are starting to put up individual prices for cups and the retail price will have to go up about 50 percent," said John Burton, principal with importer John Burton.
New York arabica coffee futures set new 20-year peaks on Thursday in the third straight day of a rally that saw prices shatter the US$3.00 a pound barrier.

Burton said roasters had worn a lot of the recent increases and importers such as his company had forward cover so that current world prices had not filtered through yet. He said he was not prepared to take further cover at current prices.

"But if these levels maintain, the market is going to have to put its prices up again," Burton said. "There will be consumer effects but it is difficult to quantify. If the market does not correct itself then the market can't keep absorbing rises and will have to pass them on."
Burton said a cup of coffee in the home would rise in price to 30 NZ cents from 20 cents.
Andrew Ellis of roaster and retailer Cafe L'Affare said his cafes were selling a cup of expresso for NZ$2 and "they will have to put it up."
He said prices of roasted beans had already gone up eight to nine percent but they would almost certainly rise again.
"It's so volatile at the moment, everyone is just standing around with their mouths open," he said.
"You can confidently say there is going to be a price increase at the retail end."
A major green bean importer, who declined to be identified, said price rises in the wholesale market had dramatically affected business.

"No one wants to pay the price, it remains to be seen whether they find the money do so," he said, adding that a general rule of thumb meant that a 10 percent price rise saw consumption fall one to two percent.
He said many importers had been caught without cover as people at the start of the year had expected the price to fall.
Importers were hoping for a frost-free Brasilian coffee growing season but if not then the price could rise three times today's prices.
